why:
In bleaching powder the connectivity is \(\mathrm{Cl^a - Ca - O - Cl^b}\), so the two chlorine atoms are in different environments and cannot carry the same oxidation number.

By the chapter's rules, an alkaline earth metal has oxidation number \(+2\), so Ca is \(+2\), and O bonded to more electropositive atoms is \(-2\).

\(\mathrm{Cl^a}\) is bonded to Ca. Calcium is the more electropositive partner, so the shared pair is assigned to chlorine and \(\mathrm{Cl^a} = -1\).

\(\mathrm{Cl^b}\) is bonded to O. Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so the shared pair is assigned to oxygen and \(\mathrm{Cl^b} = +1\).

Check: the molecule is neutral, and \((+2) + (-2) + (-1) + (+1) = 0\).

Why the others fail — "zero in each" would require both Cl atoms to be in the free element state, which they are not; "1 in each" would give a net charge of \(+2\) on a neutral molecule; and the reversed assignment \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{Cl^a}\) and \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{Cl^b}\) contradicts the electronegativity order, since it would make chlorine the more electronegative partner than calcium's neighbour oxygen and the less electronegative partner than calcium itself.

Hence the correct option is \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{Cl^a}\) and \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{Cl^b}\).

A reaction is redox only if the oxidation number of at least one element changes.

\(\mathrm{CuO + H_2 \longrightarrow Cu + H_2O}\) : Cu falls from \(+2\) to \(0\) and H rises from \(0\) to \(+1\). Redox.

\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + \ldots \longrightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\) : Fe falls from \(+3\) to \(0\), reduced by carbon monoxide, whose carbon rises from \(+2\) to \(+4\). Redox.

\(\mathrm{2K + F_2 \longrightarrow 2KF}\) : K rises from \(0\) to \(+1\) and F falls from \(0\) to \(-1\). Redox.

\(\mathrm{BaCl_2 + H_2SO_4 \longrightarrow BaSO_4 + 2HCl}\) : Ba is \(+2\), Cl is \(-1\), H is \(+1\), S is \(+6\) and O is \(-2\) on BOTH sides. Not one oxidation number moves — the ions simply exchange partners, so this is a double displacement (precipitation) reaction and not a redox reaction.

Hence the reaction that is not an example of a redox reaction is \(\mathrm{BaCl_2 + H_2SO_4 \longrightarrow BaSO_4 + 2HCl}\).
solution: [Textbook misprint: option (b) is printed as \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO_2 \longrightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\), with carbon DIOXIDE on both sides. The standard reduction of haematite uses carbon MONOXIDE, \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \longrightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\), which is a genuine redox reaction (Fe \(+3 \to 0\), C \(+2 \to +4\)); as printed the equation balances neither atoms nor electrons, since iron is reduced with nothing to oxidise. The option is preserved as printed. The answer is unaffected either way: the intended reaction is redox, so option (b) is not the one being asked for, and option (d) — a double displacement in which no oxidation number changes at all — remains the only correct choice.]

why:
A neutral compound must have the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of all its atoms equal to zero (rule 6 of the chapter). Test each formula with \(\mathrm{A} = +2\), \(\mathrm{B} = +5\), \(\mathrm{C} = -2\).

\(\mathrm{A_2(BC_3)_2}\) : \(2(+2) + 2[(+5) + 3(-2)] = 4 + 2(-1) = +2\). Not neutral.

\(\mathrm{A_3(BC_4)_2}\) : \(3(+2) + 2[(+5) + 4(-2)] = 6 + 2(-3) = 6 - 6 = 0\). Neutral.

\(\mathrm{A_3(B_4C)_2}\) : \(3(+2) + 2[4(+5) + (-2)] = 6 + 2(+18) = +42\). Not neutral.

\(\mathrm{ABC_2}\) : \((+2) + (+5) + 2(-2) = +3\). Not neutral.

Only \(\mathrm{A_3(BC_4)_2}\) balances to zero, so that is the compound the three elements can form.

Two independent conditions fix the coefficients.

Atom balance for Cr : the dichromate ion carries two Cr atoms, so \(r = 2p\).

Electron balance : in \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2\ominus}}\) each Cr is \(+6\) (since \(2x + 7(-2) = -2\)), and it becomes \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\), so each Cr gains 3 electrons and each dichromate ion gains \(2 \times 3 = 6\) electrons. Each \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\) becoming \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\) loses 1 electron. Electrons lost must equal electrons gained, so \(q = 6p\), and Fe atom balance gives \(s = q\).

Taking the smallest whole numbers, \(p = 1\), \(q = 6\), \(r = 2\), \(s = 6\).

Why the others fail — 1, 2, 6, 6 gives \(r = 6\) against only 2 Cr atoms supplied and supplies only 2 electrons where 6 are needed; 6, 1, 2, 4 leaves 12 Cr atoms on the left against 2 on the right and does not even balance Fe; 1, 2, 4, 6 fails Cr balance (\(r \neq 2p\)), Fe balance (\(s \neq q\)) and the electron count at once.

Hence the coefficients are 1, 6, 2, 6.

Track the two oxidation numbers across \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus} + 2Fe^{3\oplus} \longrightarrow Sn^{4\oplus} + 2Fe^{2\oplus}}\).

For a monoatomic ion the oxidation number is its charge, so Sn goes from \(+2\) to \(+4\) — an increase, which the chapter defines as oxidation — and Fe goes from \(+3\) to \(+2\) — a decrease, which is reduction.

So \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\) is undergoing oxidation and is the reducing agent, while \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\) is undergoing reduction and is the oxidising agent.

Why the others fail — \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\) is reduced, not oxidised; the reaction IS a redox reaction, because two oxidation numbers change; and both species cannot be oxidised, since oxidation and reduction always occur together and the two changes here are in opposite directions.

Hence the correct statement is that \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\) is undergoing oxidation.

\(\mathrm{H_2CO_3}\) is a neutral molecule, so the algebraic sum of the oxidation numbers of all its atoms is zero.

H bonded to a non-metal is \(+1\) and O is \(-2\).

\(2(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\)

\(2 + x - 6 = 0\)

\(x = +4\)

The other three values would make the molecule carry a net charge of \(-3\), \(-2\) or \(-1\) instead of being neutral, so none of them can be right.

Hence the oxidation number of carbon in carbonic acid is \(+4\).

In Stock notation the oxidation number of the metal is written as a Roman numeral in parentheses immediately after the metal's symbol, so the question reduces to finding the oxidation number of Mn in manganese dioxide, \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\).

\(\mathrm{MnO_2}\) is neutral and O is \(-2\) :

\(x + 2(-2) = 0\), so \(x = +4\).

Roman numeral IV, giving \(\mathrm{Mn(IV)O_2}\).

The other three notations claim manganese is \(+1\), \(+2\) or \(+3\); each would leave the formula unit with a net charge of \(-3\), \(-2\) or \(-1\) rather than zero.

Hence the correct Stock notation is \(\mathrm{Mn(IV)O_2}\).

The superoxide ion is \(\mathrm{O_2^{\ominus}}\), a polyatomic ion whose oxidation numbers must sum to its net charge of \(-1\) (rule 7).

Both oxygen atoms are equivalent, so if each has oxidation number \(x\) :

\(2x = -1\), giving \(x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\).

This is stated directly in the chapter's rule 3, which lists oxygen as \(-2\) in ordinary compounds, \(-1\) in peroxides and \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\) in superoxides, and it is one of the fractional oxidation numbers the chapter's "Remember" box warns about.

Why the others fail — \(-2\) is the value in an ordinary oxide and would give the ion a charge of \(-4\); \(-1\) is the peroxide value and would give \(-2\); \(0\) is the value in free \(\mathrm{O_2}\), which carries no charge at all.

Hence each oxygen in a superoxide has oxidation number \(-\dfrac{1}{2}\).

why:
The chapter's rule 5 states that the oxidation number of F is \(-1\) in all of its compounds, while Cl, Br and I usually show \(-1\) but take \(+1\) when bonded to oxygen.

The reason is that fluorine is the most electronegative element, so in any compound the shared electron pair is always assigned to fluorine and it can never be given a positive oxidation number.

Why the others fail — chlorine is \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2O}\) (both worked in this chapter's rule 5) and reaches \(+5\) in \(\mathrm{ClO_3^{\ominus}}\) and \(+7\) in \(\mathrm{ClO_4^{\ominus}}\); bromine is \(+5\) in \(\mathrm{BrO_3^{\ominus}}\); and iodine likewise takes positive values in its oxo-species. Each of those three therefore fails the word "always".

Hence the halogen that always shows oxidation state \(-1\) is fluorine.

Find the oxidation number of sulphur on each side.

In \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), which is neutral with O at \(-2\) : \(x + 2(-2) = 0\), so S is \(+4\).

In \(\mathrm{S_2Cl_2}\), which is neutral with Cl at \(-1\) (chlorine is more electronegative than sulphur) : \(2x + 2(-1) = 0\), so each S is \(+1\).

Sulphur therefore falls from \(+4\) to \(+1\). A decrease in oxidation number is, by the chapter's definition, reduction.

Why the others fail — the oxidation number decreases, so the process is not oxidation; it is not "neither", because the oxidation number does change; and it is not both, because only one element's oxidation number is being tracked here and it moves in a single direction.

Hence the process \(\mathrm{SO_2 \longrightarrow S_2Cl_2}\) is a reduction.
